newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan seen suffering as China-U.S. ties warm.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan seen suffering as China-U.S. ties warm.

text.p: Taiwan hopes its U.S. ties will not be swayed by an exchange of U.S.-China summits, but analysts said on Monday Washington may slow sales of advanced weapons to the island as U.S. ties with Taiwan's rival China warm.

Washington may not significantly shift its policy toward Taiwan, China's diplomatic rival, but a Sino-U.S. thaw could hurt Taiwan's drive for greater international status and lead the U.S. to slow advanced weapons sales to the island, analysts said.

On the fringes of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum meeting in the Philippines, U.S. President Bill Clinton and his Chinese counterpart Jiang Zemin agreed on Sunday to hold summits in Washington and Beijing in 1997 and 1998.

The planned meetings signalled the two sides were moving past the deep mutual distrust caused by Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui's visit last year to the United States, condemned by Beijing as a move to promote Taiwan's independence from China.
Since a civil war split them in 1949, China has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province not entitled to foreign ties. Both governments espouse reunification but disagree on the terms.

Although Washington switched diplomatic recognition to Beijing from Taipei in 1979, it has reserved the right to arm and even defend Taiwan in the interest of ensuring a peaceful solution to the Taiwan question.
Analysts said Washington now may be more inclined to respond to Beijing's intense pressure to stop arming Taiwan.
"Washington may slow down or delay its sales of advanced weapons to Taiwan to maintain a harmonious atmosphere with China," said Chiu Chao-lin of Taiwan's Academica Sinica.

"This is especially so since Beijing recently has not shown any forceful intimidation toward Taiwan and Washington wants a peaceful handover of Hong Kong," said Chiu, who specialises in relations between Taiwan, China and the United States.
Britain will hand Hong back to China on July 1, 1997.
Chiu said Washington could also limit high-level exchanges with Taiwan and scale back its efforts to help Taiwan enter the World Trade Organisation, which China insists on entering first.
"The best situation would be for the two sides to join the WTO at the same time. If not, the chance of Taiwan joining before China is small," said Chiu.
National Taiwan University political scientist Tim Ting said the Jiang-Clinton meeting was ominous for Taiwan.
"It seems obvious that the two big powers have reached some sort of consensus on the Taiwan issue," Ting said.

"Taiwan will suffer as tensions between China and the United States begin to thaw," he added. "Improvement of China-U.S. ties will be a setback for Taiwan's pragmatic diplomacy and its effort to expand its international living space."
Taiwanese officials were not as pessimistic.
Taiwan's APEC spokesman David Lee said in Manila he did not expect a shift in U.S. policy toward Taiwan.
"The United States will not sacrifice Taiwan's interests for the development of relations with communist China," Lee said.
"Relations between Taiwan and the United States have been systematised in past years and should not be changed just because of one or two incidents," he said.
Only 30 countries recognise Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government although the island keeps close economic relations with many countries, including the United States and even China itself.

But Taiwan-China ties show no sign of improving. Relations have yet to recover from the shock of Lee's U.S. visit and China's subsequent ban on semi-official visits and its staging of intimidating war games.
"This (summit) is not good news for Taiwan," said Ting. "Beijing will be tougher toward future talks with Taipei."
